A Deterministic O⁡(log⁡m)O(\log m)-Competitive Algorithm for
Online Minimum Cost Bipartite Matching with Delays

Tung-Wei Kuo Affiliation: Department of Computer Science, National Chengchi University, Taipei, Taiwan Email: twkuo@cs.nccu.edu.tw
Abstract

In the online Minimum cost Bipartite Perfect Matching with Delays (MBPMD) problem, mm requests and mm servers arrive over time in a metric space. An online algorithm has to match each request to a server and can postpone a matching decision by paying the delay cost. The objective is to minimize the total distance and delay cost. Azar, Chiplunkar, and Kaplan gave a randomized O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n)-competitive algorithm for metric spaces with nn points that are known in advance. For deterministic algorithms, however, the best known competitive ratio in general metric spaces was O⁡(m0.59)O(m^{0.59}), due to Azar and Jacob-Fanani. On the line, Kuo proposed the Virtual Robust Matching (VRM) algorithm and showed that it is O⁡(m​log2​m)O(\sqrt{m}\log^{2}m)-competitive.

We prove that VRM is O⁡(log⁡m)O(\log m)-competitive for the MBPMD problem in any metric space. VRM is deterministic and does not need to know the metric space or mm in advance. It is the first deterministic polylogarithmic-competitive algorithm for the MBPMD problem in general metric spaces. Unlike the previous analysis of VRM, our analysis does not rely on a geometric decomposition of the metric space. Instead, it charges the waiting time of requests over time to the edges of a fixed optimal matching.

We also extend VRM to the non-bipartite version and prove that the resulting deterministic algorithm is O⁡(log⁡m)O(\log m)-competitive. This improves the O⁡(log5⁡m)O(\log^{5}m) bound of Dufay and Wattenhofer and matches a concurrent result of Ahmadian, Chawla, Kumar, Purohit, and Zhang.

The proof that VRM is O⁡(log⁡m)O(\log m)-competitive and its non-bipartite extension were found by GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI) with almost no human input. We used Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic) to simplify and present the results. See the AI Usage and Methodology section for details. We take full responsibility for this paper.

1 Introduction

Consider a platform that matches passengers to drivers. When a passenger arrives, the platform can assign an available driver immediately or wait for a driver who is closer to the passenger. Waiting may reduce the distance traveled, but it also increases the waiting time of passengers and drivers. Thus, a natural objective is to minimize the sum of the distance and waiting time.

The above tradeoff is captured by the Minimum cost Bipartite Perfect Matching with Delays (MBPMD) problem [3, 1]. In this problem, mm requests and mm servers arrive over time in a metric space. An online algorithm has to match each request to a server, and can postpone a matching by paying the delay cost. Once a request and a server are matched, this decision cannot be changed. The objective is to minimize the total distance and delay cost. The MBPMD problem is the bipartite variant of the Minimum cost Perfect Matching with Delays (MPMD) problem [22], in which any two requests can be matched together.

We analyze algorithms using the standard notion of competitive ratio. Specifically, an online algorithm is cc-competitive if, for any input, its cost is at most cc times the cost of the optimal offline algorithm.

For the MBPMD problem, Azar, Chiplunkar, and Kaplan proposed a randomized O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n)-competitive algorithm, where nn is the number of points in the metric space, and proved that any randomized algorithm has competitive ratio Ω⁡(log1/3⁡n)\Omega(\log^{1/3}n) [3]. This lower bound was improved to Ω⁡(log⁡n/log⁡log​n)\Omega\bigl(\sqrt{\log n/\log\log n}\bigr) [1]. Both lower-bound constructions place Θ⁡(n)\Theta(n) requests on a line, so the lower bound Ω⁡(log⁡m/log⁡log​m)\Omega\bigl(\sqrt{\log m/\log\log m}\bigr) holds even on a line whose points are known in advance.

For the MPMD problem, Emek, Kutten, and Wattenhofer proposed a randomized algorithm with competitive ratio O⁡(log2⁡n+log⁡Δ)O(\log^{2}n+\log\Delta), where Δ\Delta is the aspect ratio of the metric space [22]. Azar, Chiplunkar, and Kaplan improved this ratio to O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) and proved an Ω⁡(log⁡n)\Omega(\sqrt{\log n}) lower bound for randomized algorithms [4]. The same paper that improved the MBPMD lower bound also improved this one to Ω⁡(log⁡n/log⁡log​n)\Omega(\log n/\log\log n) [1].

The known randomized algorithms first embed the metric space into a distribution over Hierarchically Separated Trees (HSTs) [24], so they need to know the metric space in advance. Recently, Coester and Huang proposed probabilistic online monotone embeddings into HSTs, which do not require prior knowledge of the metric space, but no competitive ratio for the MPMD or MBPMD problem has been derived from them, and deterministic online monotone embeddings have linear distortion [18].

In contrast, several deterministic algorithms do not require prior knowledge of the metric space. For the MPMD problem, Bienkowski, Kraska, and Schmidt proposed an O⁡(m2.46)O(m^{2.46})-competitive algorithm [17]. Bienkowski, Kraska, Liu, and Schmidt improved this ratio to O⁡(m)O(m) [16], and Azar and Jacob-Fanani obtained O⁡(ϵ−1​mlog2⁡(3/2+ϵ))O(\epsilon^{-1}m^{\log_{2}(3/2+\epsilon)}) for any fixed ϵ>0\epsilon>0, which is O⁡(m0.59)O(m^{0.59}) for small enough ϵ\epsilon [8]. Both groups adapted their algorithms to the MBPMD problem with the same competitive ratios, and the analyses are tight already on metric spaces with two points and one point, respectively.

Kuo proposed the Virtual Robust Matching (VRM) algorithm for the MBPMD problem and proved an O⁡(m​log2​m)O(\sqrt{m}\log^{2}m) competitive ratio on a line [34]. Very recently, Dufay and Wattenhofer improved the deterministic ratio for the MPMD problem from polynomial to polylogarithmic in mm. Their O⁡(log5⁡m)O(\log^{5}m)-competitive algorithm does not need to know the metric space or mm in advance [21]. However, they noted that several key parts of their approach, specifically the greedy algorithm and the component decomposition, do not naturally extend to the bipartite case [21].

Concurrently with and independently of our work, Ahmadian, Chawla, Kumar, Purohit, and Zhang obtained a deterministic O⁡(log⁡m)O(\log m)-competitive algorithm for the MPMD problem that also does not need to know the metric space or mm in advance. They noted that their approach does not extend directly to the bipartite case and left a logarithmic competitive ratio for this case as an open question [5]. Thus, prior to our work, no polylogarithmic competitive ratio was known for the MBPMD problem without prior knowledge of the metric space.

1.1 Our Contribution and Techniques

In this paper, we prove that the VRM algorithm is O⁡(log⁡m)O(\log m)-competitive for the MBPMD problem in any metric space. Specifically, let ALG\operatorname{ALG} be the cost of the online algorithm and let OPT\operatorname{OPT} be the cost of the optimal offline algorithm, which knows the entire input. We have the following result.

Theorem 1.1.

For every fixed γ>1\gamma>1, the VRM algorithm with parameter γ\gamma described in Section 3 is a deterministic online algorithm for the MBPMD problem in any metric space, and on every input, its cost satisfies

ALG≤(2+2​γγ−1)​[1+(γ+1)​(1+ln⁡m)]​OPT.\operatorname{ALG}\leq\left(2+\frac{2\gamma}{\gamma-1}\right)\bigl[1+(\gamma+1)(1+\ln m)\bigr]\operatorname{OPT}.

In particular, for γ=2\gamma=2, the VRM algorithm is (24+18​ln⁡m)(24+18\ln m)-competitive. Moreover, the algorithm does not need to know the metric space or mm in advance.

Theorem 1.1 gives the first deterministic algorithm with a polylogarithmic competitive ratio for the MBPMD problem in general metric spaces. In particular, it gives a logarithmic competitive ratio for the bipartite problem, which [5] leaves open.

The RM algorithm.

VRM is based on the Robust Matching (RM) algorithm proposed by Raghvendra for the online Minimum cost Bipartite Perfect Matching (MBPM) problem [42]. In the MBPM problem, all servers arrive in the beginning, and a request must be matched immediately after it arrives. The objective is the total distance of the matching.

The RM algorithm maintains an offline matching MOFFM^{\mathrm{OFF}} and an online matching MRMM^{\textnormal{RM}}, which is the real output matching. When a request rr arrives, the algorithm computes an MOFFM^{\mathrm{OFF}}-augmenting path PrP_{r} from rr to a free server ss that minimizes the γ\gamma-net-cost, which is γ\gamma times the total length of the edges added to MOFFM^{\mathrm{OFF}} minus the total length of the edges removed from MOFFM^{\mathrm{OFF}}.11 1 In [42], this cost is referred to as the tt-net-cost. However, because tt denotes time in this paper, we change tt-net-cost to γ\gamma-net-cost. It then adds the pair r​srs to MRMM^{\textnormal{RM}} and augments MOFFM^{\mathrm{OFF}} by PrP_{r}. Nayyar and Raghvendra proved that the competitive ratio of RM is O⁡(m1−1/d​log2​m)O(m^{1-1/d}\log^{2}m) in dd-dimensional Euclidean space [40], and Raghvendra proved that RM is O⁡(log⁡m)O(\log m)-competitive on a line [43].

The VRM algorithm.

The MBPMD problem differs from the MBPM problem in two respects: servers arrive over time, and a request can wait. To handle the arrival times, VRM works in the time-augmented (TA) metric. In the TA metric, the distance between two items (called their TA distance) is their distance in the original metric space plus the difference of their arrival times [17, 8, 34].

To decide when to match a request, the original VRM algorithm introduces a Moving Virtual (MV) server for every request. The MV server of a request stays at the location of the request and moves forward in time, so its TA distance to the request is the time elapsed since the request arrived. Consider a request rr. An augmenting path of rr is real if all servers in the path are real. It is virtual if its last edge is from some request pp to pp’s MV server, and all the other servers in the path are real.

For example, the edge from rr to rr’s MV server is a virtual augmenting path of rr. Its γ\gamma-net-cost is γ\gamma times the waiting time of rr, so it is zero when rr arrives and increases over time. Among the real augmenting paths of rr, let PrP_{r} be one with minimum γ\gamma-net-cost. Define P~r\widetilde{P}_{r} similarly for the virtual augmenting paths of rr. The request rr is matched when the γ\gamma-net-cost of PrP_{r} becomes less than or equal to that of P~r\widetilde{P}_{r}.

Kuo proved that the edge from rr to rr’s MV server always has the minimum γ\gamma-net-cost among the virtual augmenting paths of rr [34, Lemma 4.1].22 2 The lemma is stated there for γ=3\gamma=3 on the line, but its proof needs only γ≥1\gamma\geq 1 and does not use the line structure. Hence, it holds for every γ>1\gamma>1 in every metric space. Thus, rr is matched when the γ\gamma-net-cost of PrP_{r} becomes less than or equal to γ\gamma times the waiting time of rr. In Section 3, we present this simplified algorithm, which we take as the definition of VRM in this paper.

The analysis.

Let WRW_{R} be the total waiting time of requests under VRM. Our analysis has two steps. The first step bounds the total cost of the algorithm, including the distance cost and the delay cost of both requests and servers, by (2+2​γγ−1)​WR(2+\frac{2\gamma}{\gamma-1})W_{R}. The proof of this step is similar to the analysis of VRM [34].

The second step is a charging argument, in which we charge WRW_{R} to the optimal cost. We fix an optimal matching M∗M^{*}. At any time tt, the symmetric difference of M∗M^{*} and MOFFM^{\mathrm{OFF}} contains an alternating path from each free request rr to a server. We call this path the optimal path of rr and the server its terminal server. At every moment, we charge the waiting cost of rr to the edges of M∗M^{*} on its optimal path. There are two cases, according to whether the terminal server of the path has arrived.

  1. 1.

    If the terminal server ss has not arrived, we charge the waiting cost of rr to the last edge e=p​se=ps of the path, where pp is the request preceding ss on the path. The optimal path is an MOFFM^{\mathrm{OFF}}-augmenting path, so ee is not in MOFFM^{\mathrm{OFF}} and hence is an edge of M∗M^{*}. Because the optimal paths of distinct free requests share no edge, ee is charged by at most one request at any time. Moreover, ee is charged only after pp arrives and before ss arrives. Hence, the total charge to ee is at most the difference of the arrival times of pp and ss, and summing over the edges of M∗M^{*} shows that the total charge in this case is at most OPT\operatorname{OPT}.

  2. 2.

    If the terminal server has arrived, then the optimal path is a valid augmenting path that the algorithm could use. Because rr is waiting, the γ\gamma-net-cost of this path is at least γ\gamma times the waiting time of rr. Consequently, the waiting time of rr is at most the total length D∗D^{*} of the edges of M∗M^{*} on the path, and every vertex on the path arrived within the last (γ+1)​D∗(\gamma+1)D^{*} time units. We charge the waiting cost of rr to the edges of M∗M^{*} on the path, in proportion to their lengths. Each edge ee of M∗M^{*}, of length D⁡(e)D(e), receives a total charge of at most (γ+1)​(OPT/m+D⁡(e)​ln⁡m)(\gamma+1)({\operatorname{OPT}}/m+D(e)\ln m) in this case.

Summing over the mm edges of M∗M^{*}, the total charge in the second case is at most (γ+1)​(1+ln⁡m)​OPT(\gamma+1)(1+\ln m)\operatorname{OPT}. Thus, WR≤[1+(γ+1)​(1+ln⁡m)]​OPTW_{R}\leq[1+(\gamma+1)(1+\ln m)]\operatorname{OPT}, and Theorem 1.1 follows from the first step.

Extension to the MPMD problem.

In Section 5, we extend VRM and its analysis to the MPMD problem. We call the resulting algorithm non-bipartite VRM. By Theorem 5.1, it is (28+24​ln⁡m)(28+24\ln m)-competitive for γ=2\gamma=2, where 2​m2m is the number of requests. This improves the O⁡(log5⁡m)O(\log^{5}m) bound of [21] to O⁡(log⁡m)O(\log m). Like VRM, it is deterministic and does not need to know the metric space or mm in advance. In concurrent work, Ahmadian, Chawla, Kumar, Purohit, and Zhang obtained the same asymptotic bound [5].

The extension requires two main changes. First, because there are no servers, both endpoints of an augmenting path are requests, and each of them can initiate an augmentation. Thus, both endpoints of an optimal path can be free requests that charge the edges of M∗M^{*} on the path at the same time, which at most doubles the charge rate of each such edge. Second, in the bipartite case, VRM computes the minimum augmenting path PrP_{r} of each request rr as a shortest path in a directed graph whose orientation relies on the bipartition. In the non-bipartite case, we instead compute PrP_{r} from minimum-weight perfect matchings in general graphs.

1.2 Other Related Work

Special metric spaces.

When the metric space is known in advance and forms a tree of height hh, deterministic O⁡(h)O(h)-competitive algorithms are known for both the MPMD and the MBPMD problems [4, 3, 1]. On a line with nn points, however, this gives only an O⁡(n)O(n) bound. When n=2n=2, Emek, Shapiro, and Wang proposed a deterministic 33-competitive algorithm for the MPMD problem and proved that 33 is optimal for deterministic algorithms [23]. For randomized algorithms, a 22-competitive algorithm is known for this case, and it is optimal [29].

Online metric matching without delays.

VRM is based on the RM algorithm for the MBPM problem. For this problem, the optimal deterministic competitive ratio in general metric spaces is 2​m−12m-1 [33, 31]. Randomized algorithms achieve O⁡(log2⁡m)O(\log^{2}m) in general [14] and O⁡(log⁡m)O(\log m) for doubling metrics [27]. Nayyar and Raghvendra showed that the RM algorithm is O⁡(m1−1/d​log2​m)O(m^{1-1/d}\log^{2}m)-competitive when the servers span a space of doubling dimension dd [40], and Raghvendra showed that it is O⁡(log⁡m)O(\log m)-competitive on a line [43]. No randomized algorithm on a line is o⁡(log⁡m)o(\sqrt{\log m})-competitive [41]. In contrast, no algorithm has a bounded competitive ratio for a non-bipartite variant, even on a line under random-order arrivals [2]. In this variant, all requests arrive online, and each arriving request is either matched to a waiting request or joins a waiting pool at no cost. Online matching has also been studied with recourse [26, 37], with maximization objectives, and under other arrival models [36, 30].

Variants of matching with delays.

Some variants change how requests arrive. Under Poisson arrivals, Mari, Pawłowski, Ren, and Sankowski proved that the greedy algorithm that matches two requests as soon as their total waiting time exceeds their distance is O⁡(1)O(1)-competitive in expectation for the MPMD problem [38]. Against adversarial arrivals, however, its competitive ratio is Ω⁡(mlog2⁡1.5)\Omega(m^{\log_{2}1.5}), where log2⁡1.5≈0.585\log_{2}1.5\approx 0.585, because it reduces to the greedy heuristic for minimum-cost perfect matching [44] when all requests arrive simultaneously.

Other variants change how many requests are matched together. Melnyk, Wang, and Wattenhofer introduced kk-way matching with delays, in which requests are matched in groups of kk, and gave a randomized algorithm on a class of metrics called HH-metrics [39]. For this problem on HH-metrics, Kakimura and Nakayoshi gave a deterministic O⁡(m​k2)O(mk^{2})-competitive primal-dual algorithm, where mm is the number of requests [32]. Ahmadian, Chawla, Kumar, Purohit, and Zhang gave a deterministic O⁡(k​log⁡m)O(k\log m)-competitive algorithm when the cost of a group is the sum of the distances between its requests, and a deterministic O⁡(k3​log⁡m)O(k^{3}\log m)-competitive algorithm for general HH-metrics [5].

Some variants replace the waiting time with a different delay cost. For convex delay costs tαt^{\alpha} with α>1\alpha>1 on uniform metric spaces with nn points, the deterministic competitive ratio is Θ⁡(n)\Theta(n) [35]. For concave delay costs, Azar, Ren, and Vainstein gave a randomized O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n)-competitive algorithm based on HSTs for both the MPMD and the MBPMD problems [10]. Deryckere and Umboh gave a deterministic O⁡(m)O(m)-competitive primal-dual algorithm for the MPMD problem with concave delays in general metric spaces [20]. Ahmadian, Chawla, Kumar, Purohit, and Zhang adapted their own MPMD algorithm to concave delay functions that are known in advance and unbounded, and obtained a deterministic O⁡(log⁡m)O(\log m)-competitive algorithm [5].

Deryckere and Umboh also introduced set delays, where the delay cost at each time is a function of the set of unmatched requests [20]. For size-based delays, where this cost depends only on the number of unmatched requests, the deterministic competitive ratio is Θ⁡(2n)\Theta(2^{n}) [28].

Other online problems with delays.

The study of online problems with delays originates from the TCP acknowledgment problem [19]. For online service with delays and network design with delays, randomized polylogarithmic competitive ratios were first obtained via HSTs [7, 11], and deterministic ones were then obtained without tree embeddings [12, 45]. The MBPMD problem now follows the same pattern: its known randomized algorithms use HSTs, and Theorem 1.1 gives a deterministic O⁡(log⁡m)O(\log m)-competitive algorithm without tree embeddings. Other problems with delays or deadlines include multi-level aggregation [13, 15], set cover with delay [6], caching with time windows [25], and list update with delays [9].

2 Preliminaries

2.1 Problem Definition

Let (X,d)(X,d) be a metric space. Let RR and SS be the request set and the server set, respectively, where |R|=|S|=m|R|=|S|=m. For each request or server v∈R∪Sv\in R\cup S, let xv∈Xx_{v}\in X and av≥0a_{v}\geq 0 be its location and arrival time, respectively. We call requests and servers items. When vv arrives, the algorithm learns its type, its location, and its distances to all items that arrive by time ava_{v}. The algorithm does not know future arrivals or their locations, and it does not know the metric space or mm in advance.

The algorithm must eventually output a perfect matching MM between RR and SS. If it matches rr to ss at time tr​st_{rs}, then tr​s≥max⁡{ar,as}t_{rs}\geq\max\{a_{r},a_{s}\}, and this decision cannot be changed. The objective is to minimize the total distance of the matched pairs plus the total waiting time of all items, that is,

min⁡∑r​s∈MM,{tr​s}r​s∈M⁡(d⁡(xr,xs)+(tr​s−ar)+(tr​s−as)).\min_{M,\,\{t_{rs}\}_{rs\in M}}\ \sum_{rs\in M}\bigl(d(x_{r},x_{s})+(t_{rs}-a_{r})+(t_{rs}-a_{s})\bigr). (2.1)

2.2 Matchings and Augmenting Paths

A matching MM between RR and SS is a set of vertex-disjoint edges between RR and SS. An item is saturated by MM if it is an endpoint of an edge in MM. Otherwise, it is free in MM. An MM-alternating path alternates between edges in MM and edges not in MM. An MM-alternating path is MM-augmenting if neither endpoint is saturated by MM. We identify a path with its edge set, and for two edge sets AA and BB, we write A△B=(A∖B)∪(B∖A)A\mathbin{\triangle}B=(A\setminus B)\cup(B\setminus A) for their symmetric difference.

An MM-augmenting path PP can be used to enlarge MM. We view PP as a directed path from a free request to a free server, and write ter⁡(P)\ter(P) for its last vertex. Following PP from its free request, we update MM as follows:

  1. 1.

    If an edge of PP goes from a request to a server, it is added to MM.

  2. 2.

    If an edge of PP goes from a server to a request, it is removed from MM.

The resulting matching is M△PM\mathbin{\triangle}P, and its size is |M|+1|M|+1.

2.3 The Time-Augmented Distance

We define the time-augmented (TA) distance between items uu and vv as

D⁡(u,v)=d⁡(xu,xv)+|au−av|.D(u,v)=d(x_{u},x_{v})+|a_{u}-a_{v}|. (2.2)

For an edge e=u​ve=uv, define D⁡(e)=D⁡(u,v)D(e)=D(u,v), and for any edge set FF, define D⁡(F)=∑e∈FD⁡(e)D(F)=\sum_{e\in F}D(e). The TA distance was used in [17, 8, 34]. The following lemma relates it to the optimal cost.

Lemma 2.1 ([8]).

If M∗M^{*} is a minimum-cost perfect matching between RR and SS under DD, then OPT=D⁡(M∗)\operatorname{OPT}=D(M^{*}).

3 The VRM Algorithm

In this section, we describe the VRM algorithm [34] for any metric space, in the simplified form discussed in Section 1.1. Let γ>1\gamma>1 be a parameter that remains fixed throughout the execution. We first define the augmenting paths used by the algorithm (Section 3.1) and then state the readiness rule, which decides when a free request is matched along its augmenting path (Section 3.2). Section 3.3 describes the algorithm, and Section 3.4 states the basic properties used in the analysis.

Following the notation of VRM [34], the algorithm maintains an offline matching MOFFM^{\mathrm{OFF}} and an online matching MVRMM^{\mathrm{VRM}}, which is the real output matching. The offline matching is an auxiliary matching on the items that have arrived. Both matchings are initially empty. The algorithm can change edges in MOFFM^{\mathrm{OFF}}, but cannot change a pair that has been added to MVRMM^{\mathrm{VRM}}.

We will see in Section 3.3 that MOFFM^{\mathrm{OFF}} and MVRMM^{\mathrm{VRM}} always saturate the same items. An item is free at time tt if it has arrived and is not saturated by MOFFM^{\mathrm{OFF}} (equivalently, by MVRMM^{\mathrm{VRM}}) at time tt. Let Rfree​(t)R_{\mathrm{free}}(t) be the set of free requests at time tt. The set Rfree​(t)R_{\mathrm{free}}(t) does not contain requests that have not arrived. For an arrived item vv, its age at time tt is age⁡(v,t)=t−av\operatorname{age}(v,t)=t-a_{v}. For a free request, the age is its current waiting time.

3.1 Minimum Net-Cost Augmenting Paths

Consider the complete bipartite graph HH on the requests and servers that have arrived. For each request rr and server ss, we assign the direction and weight of their edge as follows:

{r⟶s,weight ​γ​D​(r,s),r​s∉MOFF,s⟶r,weight −D⁡(r,s),r​s∈MOFF.\begin{cases}r\longrightarrow s,\quad\text{weight }\gamma D(r,s),&rs\notin M^{\mathrm{OFF}},\\ s\longrightarrow r,\quad\text{weight }{-D(r,s)},&rs\in M^{\mathrm{OFF}}.\end{cases}

A directed path from a free request to a free server in HH is an MOFFM^{\mathrm{OFF}}-augmenting path whose vertices have all arrived.

For a matching MM and an MM-augmenting path PP, define

DM+​(P)=D(P∖M),D−M(P)=D(P∩M),φM​(P)=γ​DM+​(P)−DM−​(P).\begin{split}D^{+}_{M}(P)&=D(P\setminus M),\qquad D^{-}_{M}(P)=D(P\cap M),\\ \varphi_{M}(P)&=\gamma D^{+}_{M}(P)-D^{-}_{M}(P).\end{split} (3.1)

We call φM​(P)\varphi_{M}(P) the γ\gamma-net-cost of PP. Specifically, it is γ\gamma times the total TA distance of the edges added to MM, minus the total TA distance of the edges removed from MM. For an MOFFM^{\mathrm{OFF}}-augmenting path PP from a free request to a free server, φMOFF​(P)\varphi_{M^{\mathrm{OFF}}}(P) is also the total weight of PP in HH.

For each free request rr, let PrP_{r} be an MOFFM^{\mathrm{OFF}}-augmenting path that minimizes the γ\gamma-net-cost among all MOFFM^{\mathrm{OFF}}-augmenting paths from rr to a free server. We call PrP_{r} the minimum augmenting path of rr, and let φr=φMOFF​(Pr)\varphi_{r}=\varphi_{M^{\mathrm{OFF}}}(P_{r}) be the minimum γ\gamma-net-cost of rr. Because the γ\gamma-net-cost of such a path equals its weight in HH, PrP_{r} is a shortest path from rr to the set of free servers in HH, and φr\varphi_{r} is its length. If no free server exists, then no such path exists, and we set φr=+∞\varphi_{r}=+\infty. We prove the following lemma in Appendix A. Its proof is similar to the corresponding proofs for RM [42] and VRM [34].

Lemma 3.1.

The graph HH has no negative cycle at any state.

Thus, shortest paths exist and can be chosen simple, and PrP_{r} is well defined.

3.2 The Readiness Rule

A free request rr is ready at time tt if

γ⁡(t−ar)≥φr,\gamma(t-a_{r})\geq\varphi_{r}, (3.2)

that is, if its waiting time is at least its minimum γ\gamma-net-cost divided by γ\gamma. When rr is ready, the algorithm adds r​srs to MVRMM^{\mathrm{VRM}}, where s=ter⁡(Pr)s=\ter(P_{r}), and augments MOFFM^{\mathrm{OFF}} by PrP_{r}. This is the simplified readiness rule of VRM discussed in Section 1.1 [34, Section 4.1, Implication 1].

Whenever PrP_{r} is updated at time tt, the algorithm checks Eq. (3.2). If rr is not ready, its ready time is

trrdy=t+φr−γ⁡(t−ar)γ=ar+φrγ,t_{r}^{\mathrm{rdy}}=t+\frac{\varphi_{r}-\gamma(t-a_{r})}{\gamma}=a_{r}+\frac{\varphi_{r}}{\gamma}, (3.3)

and trrdy=+∞t_{r}^{\mathrm{rdy}}=+\infty if φr=+∞\varphi_{r}=+\infty.

3.3 Algorithm Description

Following the event description of VRM [34, Section 4], the execution of the algorithm is driven by three types of events:

  1. 1.

    Event RA: A request rr arrives. Compute the minimum augmenting path PrP_{r}, the minimum γ\gamma-net-cost φr\varphi_{r}, and the ready time of rr. Because rr is free, it cannot be an interior vertex of another free request’s augmenting path. Thus, the minimum augmenting paths and ready times of the other free requests do not change.

  2. 2.

    Event SA: A server ss arrives. Update the minimum augmenting paths, the minimum γ\gamma-net-costs, and the ready times of all free requests.

  3. 3.

    Event AU: A free request rr is ready. Let s=ter⁡(Pr)s=\ter(P_{r}). Add r​srs to MVRMM^{\mathrm{VRM}} with matching time equal to the current time, and augment MOFFM^{\mathrm{OFF}} by PrP_{r}, that is, set MOFF←MOFF△PrM^{\mathrm{OFF}}\leftarrow M^{\mathrm{OFF}}\mathbin{\triangle}P_{r}. Then update the minimum augmenting paths, the minimum γ\gamma-net-costs, and the ready times of all remaining free requests.

By the design of the algorithm, MOFFM^{\mathrm{OFF}} and MVRMM^{\mathrm{VRM}} always saturate the same items, and every output decision is feasible. Every free request has an edge to every free server in HH, so φr<+∞\varphi_{r}<+\infty whenever a free server exists. After the last arrival, there are m−|MOFF|m-|M^{\mathrm{OFF}}| free requests and m−|MOFF|m-|M^{\mathrm{OFF}}| free servers, so a free server exists whenever a free request does. Hence, after the last arrival, every free request has a finite ready time, and the algorithm eventually outputs a perfect matching.

Ties among simultaneous events and among minimum augmenting paths are broken by an arbitrary but fixed rule, which makes the algorithm deterministic, and our analysis holds for every such rule.

3.4 Basic Properties

The analysis uses the readiness rule in two ways. First, a request rr is matched only when it is ready. Thus, if rr is matched at time trt_{r} along the path PrP_{r} with γ\gamma-net-cost φr\varphi_{r}, then

φr≤γ⁡(tr−ar).\varphi_{r}\leq\gamma(t_{r}-a_{r}). (3.4)

Second, while a request waits, it is not ready. To make this precise, we use the following notion.

Definition 3.2.

A time tt is stable if it is not an event time, that is, no item arrives and no augmentation is performed at time tt.

Consider a stable time tt, a free request rr, and an MOFFM^{\mathrm{OFF}}-augmenting path PP from rr to a free server. Because φr\varphi_{r} is the minimum γ\gamma-net-cost of such paths, we have φMOFF​(P)≥φr\varphi_{M^{\mathrm{OFF}}}(P)\geq\varphi_{r}. Because tt is stable, Event AU does not occur at time tt, so no free request is ready at time tt. In particular, φr>γ⁡(t−ar)\varphi_{r}>\gamma(t-a_{r}) by Eq. (3.2). Therefore, we have the following lemma.

Lemma 3.3.

At every stable time tt, no free request is ready. In particular, every MOFFM^{\mathrm{OFF}}-augmenting path PP from any free request rr to any free server satisfies

φMOFF​(P)≥φr>γ⁡(t−ar).\varphi_{M^{\mathrm{OFF}}}(P)\geq\varphi_{r}>\gamma(t-a_{r}).

4 Analysis

In this section, we prove Theorem 1.1. Let trt_{r} be the time when request rr is matched by VRM, and let

WR=∑r∈R(tr−ar)=∫0∞|Rfree​(t)|​𝑑tW_{R}=\sum_{r\in R}(t_{r}-a_{r})=\int_{0}^{\infty}|R_{\mathrm{free}}(t)|\,dt (4.1)

be the total waiting time of requests. The second equality follows because each free request incurs one unit of waiting cost per unit of time. The proof has two steps. In Section 4.1, we show that ALG≤(2+2​γγ−1)​WR\operatorname{ALG}\leq(2+\frac{2\gamma}{\gamma-1})W_{R}. In Sections 4.2–4.4, we charge the waiting cost of every request, at every stable time, to the edges of a fixed optimal matching and bound the charge that each edge receives. Section 4.5 sums these bounds to show that WR≤[1+(γ+1)​(1+ln⁡m)]​OPTW_{R}\leq[1+(\gamma+1)(1+\ln m)]\operatorname{OPT} and combines the two steps.

4.1 Bounding the Total Cost by the Total Waiting Time of Requests

The following lemma relates WRW_{R} to the total cost of the algorithm, which includes the distance cost and the delay cost of both requests and servers.

as desired. ∎

4.2 Optimal Paths and the Charging Scheme

To bound WRW_{R}, we compare the offline matching with a fixed optimal matching under the TA distance. Let M∗M^{*} be a minimum-cost perfect matching between RR and SS under DD, so that D⁡(M∗)=OPTD(M^{*})=\operatorname{OPT} by Lemma 2.1. Let MtM_{t} be the offline matching at time tt. Consider a free request rr at time tt. Because rr is not saturated by MtM_{t} and M∗M^{*} is perfect, the component of Mt△M∗M_{t}\mathbin{\triangle}M^{*} containing rr is an MtM_{t}-augmenting path from rr to a server. We call this path the optimal path of rr at time tt, denote it by Pr∗​(t)P^{*}_{r}(t), and call its last vertex the terminal server. The terminal server is not saturated by MtM_{t}, so it is either free or not yet arrived.

Lemma 4.2.

At any time tt, the optimal paths of different free requests share no edge, and every interior vertex of an optimal path has arrived.

Proof.

The optimal paths of different free requests are different components of Mt△M∗M_{t}\mathbin{\triangle}M^{*}, so they share no edge. Next, an optimal path alternates between edges of M∗M^{*} and edges of MtM_{t}, so every interior vertex is incident to an edge of MtM_{t}. Because MtM_{t} is a matching on the items that have arrived, every interior vertex has arrived. ∎

By Lemma 4.2, the only vertex of Pr∗​(t)P^{*}_{r}(t) that may not have arrived is its terminal server.

The charging scheme.

There are at most 2​m2m arrival times and at most mm augmentations, so there are only finitely many event times. Thus, the waiting cost incurred at event times is zero, and it suffices to charge the waiting cost at stable times. We consider a stable time tt and a free request rr. The waiting cost of rr increases at rate one, and we charge it as follows.

  • •

    Case 1: the terminal server of Pr∗​(t)P^{*}_{r}(t) has not arrived. We charge the waiting cost of rr to the last edge of Pr∗​(t)P^{*}_{r}(t). Because the terminal server is not saturated by MtM_{t}, this edge is not in MtM_{t}. It lies in Mt△M∗M_{t}\mathbin{\triangle}M^{*}, so it is an edge of M∗M^{*}. By Lemma 4.2, at any time, each edge is charged by at most one request. Let W1W_{1} be the total waiting cost charged in this case over all requests and over time. Section 4.3 shows that W1≤OPTW_{1}\leq\operatorname{OPT}.

  • •

    Case 2: the terminal server of Pr∗​(t)P^{*}_{r}(t) has arrived. Let D∗=D⁡(Pr∗​(t)∩M∗)D^{*}=D(P^{*}_{r}(t)\cap M^{*}) be the total TA distance of the edges of M∗M^{*} on Pr∗​(t)P^{*}_{r}(t). For each edge e∈Pr∗​(t)∩M∗e\in P^{*}_{r}(t)\cap M^{*}, we charge the waiting cost of rr to ee at rate

    D⁡(e)D∗.\frac{D(e)}{D^{*}}. (4.3)

    Lemma 4.4 in Section 4.4 gives D∗≥age⁡(r,t)D^{*}\geq\operatorname{age}(r,t), and age⁡(r,t)>0\operatorname{age}(r,t)>0 because no item arrives at the stable time tt. Thus, the rate is well defined. Figure 1(a) illustrates this rule. By Lemma 4.2, at any time, each edge is charged by at most one request. For each edge e∈M∗e\in M^{*}, let qe​(t)q_{e}(t) be the charge rate assigned to ee in this case at a stable time tt, with qe​(t)=0q_{e}(t)=0 at event times.

Every unit of WRW_{R} is charged by exactly one of the above rules. Therefore,

WR=W1+∑e∈M∗∫0∞qe​(t)​𝑑t.W_{R}=W_{1}+\sum_{e\in M^{*}}\int_{0}^{\infty}q_{e}(t)\,dt. (4.4)

It remains to bound W1W_{1} and ∫0∞qe​(t)​𝑑t\int_{0}^{\infty}q_{e}(t)\,dt for every e∈M∗e\in M^{*}. We treat these bounds in Sections 4.3 and 4.4.

4.3 Case 1: The Terminal Server Has Not Arrived

Lemma 4.3.

The total waiting cost charged in Case 1 satisfies W1≤OPTW_{1}\leq\operatorname{OPT}.

Proof.

In Case 1, a free request charges its waiting cost to the last edge of its optimal path. Fix an edge e=p​s∈M∗e=ps\in M^{*} that is charged in Case 1, where p∈Rp\in R and s∈Ss\in S. If a free request rr charges ee in Case 1 at time tt, then ss is the terminal server of Pr∗​(t)P^{*}_{r}(t), so ss has not arrived at time tt. By Lemma 4.2, pp has arrived, since it is rr or an interior vertex of Pr∗​(t)P^{*}_{r}(t). Thus, ap≤t<asa_{p}\leq t<a_{s}, so pp arrives before ss, and ee is charged only during [ap,as][a_{p},a_{s}].

An edge of M∗M^{*} that is never charged in Case 1 contributes nothing, so summing over all edges of M∗M^{*} gives W1≤∑p​s∈M∗D⁡(p,s)=OPTW_{1}\leq\sum_{ps\in M^{*}}D(p,s)=\operatorname{OPT}. ∎

For γ=2\gamma=2, the coefficient is 6​(4+3​ln⁡m)=24+18​ln⁡m6(4+3\ln m)=24+18\ln m. Finally, the algorithm does not need to know the metric space or mm in advance, since M∗M^{*}, OPT\operatorname{OPT}, and mm are used only in the analysis.

5 Extension to Non-Bipartite Matching with Delays

In this section, we extend VRM and its analysis to the MPMD problem, in which any two requests can be matched. Let RR be the set of requests, which arrive over time in a metric space, and let |R|=2​m|R|=2m, so that mm is the number of pairs in a perfect matching. We use the same notation for their locations xvx_{v}, arrival times ava_{v}, and TA distances D⁡(u,v)=d⁡(xu,xv)+|au−av|D(u,v)=d(x_{u},x_{v})+|a_{u}-a_{v}|. The objective is to minimize the total distance of the matched pairs plus the total waiting time of all requests. Lemma 2.1 also holds for the MPMD problem [8]. That is, D⁡(M∗)=OPTD(M^{*})=\operatorname{OPT} for every minimum-cost perfect matching M∗M^{*} on RR under DD.

We call our extension non-bipartite VRM. Because there are no servers, both endpoints of an augmenting path are requests, and each of them can initiate an augmentation. The analysis uses the same optimal paths and charging scheme as in Section 4. The main difference is that we now charge the waiting time of both endpoints of an optimal path. Thus, two requests can charge the same edge of M∗M^{*} at the same time. We obtain the following result.

Theorem 5.1.

For every fixed γ>1\gamma>1, the non-bipartite VRM algorithm described below is a deterministic online algorithm for the MPMD problem in any metric space. On every input, its cost satisfies

ALG≤2​γγ−1​[1+2​(γ+1)​(1+ln⁡m)]​OPT.\operatorname{ALG}\leq\frac{2\gamma}{\gamma-1}\bigl[1+2(\gamma+1)(1+\ln m)\bigr]\operatorname{OPT}.

In particular, for γ=2\gamma=2, it is (28+24​ln⁡m)(28+24\ln m)-competitive. The algorithm does not need to know the metric space or mm in advance.

5.1 The Algorithm

As in Section 3, the algorithm maintains an offline matching MOFFM^{\mathrm{OFF}} and an online matching MVRMM^{\mathrm{VRM}}, both initially empty. A request is free at time tt if it has arrived and is not saturated by MOFFM^{\mathrm{OFF}} (equivalently, by MVRMM^{\mathrm{VRM}}) at time tt. Because any two requests can be matched, MOFFM^{\mathrm{OFF}} can contain an edge between any two distinct arrived requests. An MOFFM^{\mathrm{OFF}}-augmenting path is a simple alternating path between two distinct requests that are free in MOFFM^{\mathrm{OFF}}. For a matching MM and an edge set FF, define

φM​(F)=γ​D​(F∖M)−D⁡(F∩M).\varphi_{M}(F)=\gamma D(F\setminus M)-D(F\cap M).

We call φM​(F)\varphi_{M}(F) the γ\gamma-net-cost of FF. For an MM-augmenting path, this agrees with Eq. (3.1).

For each free request uu, let PuP_{u} be an MOFFM^{\mathrm{OFF}}-augmenting path that minimizes the γ\gamma-net-cost among all MOFFM^{\mathrm{OFF}}-augmenting paths from uu to another free request. We call PuP_{u} the minimum augmenting path of uu, and let φu=φMOFF​(Pu)\varphi_{u}=\varphi_{M^{\mathrm{OFF}}}(P_{u}) be the minimum γ\gamma-net-cost of uu. If there is no other free request, we set φu=+∞\varphi_{u}=+\infty. Otherwise, the edge from uu to another free request is a candidate, and there are only finitely many simple paths on the arrived requests. Thus, PuP_{u} is well defined.

A free request uu is ready at time tt if

γ⁡(t−au)≥φu.\gamma(t-a_{u})\geq\varphi_{u}. (5.1)

Whenever PuP_{u} is updated, the algorithm checks Eq. (5.1). If uu is not ready, its ready time is au+φu/γa_{u}+\varphi_{u}/\gamma, which is +∞+\infty if φu=+∞\varphi_{u}=+\infty.

The execution of the algorithm is driven by two types of events:

  1. 1.

    Event RA: A request vv arrives. Update the minimum augmenting paths, the minimum γ\gamma-net-costs, and the ready times of all free requests, including vv. Because vv can be the other endpoint of the minimum augmenting paths of the other free requests, these requests must also be updated, unlike in Event RA of Section 3.3.

  2. 2.

    Event AU: A free request uu is ready. Let vv be the other endpoint of PuP_{u}. Add u​vuv to MVRMM^{\mathrm{VRM}} with matching time equal to the current time, and set MOFF←MOFF△PuM^{\mathrm{OFF}}\leftarrow M^{\mathrm{OFF}}\mathbin{\triangle}P_{u}. Then update the minimum augmenting paths, the minimum γ\gamma-net-costs, and the ready times of all remaining free requests.

Ties among simultaneous events and among the choices in Steps 1 and 2 of Section 5.2 are broken by an arbitrary but fixed rule, which makes the algorithm deterministic, and our analysis holds for every such rule. The matchings MOFFM^{\mathrm{OFF}} and MVRMM^{\mathrm{VRM}} always saturate the same requests, so every output decision is feasible, and the algorithm eventually outputs a perfect matching.

As in Definition 3.2, a time is stable if no request arrives and no augmentation is performed at that time. For an arrived request vv, let age⁡(v,t)=t−av\operatorname{age}(v,t)=t-a_{v} be its age at time tt. Consider a stable time tt and an MOFFM^{\mathrm{OFF}}-augmenting path PP between free requests uu and vv. Because PP can be traversed in either direction, it is a candidate for the minimum augmenting paths of both uu and vv. Because tt is stable, Event AU does not occur at time tt, so no free request is ready at time tt. Thus, by Eq. (5.1), we have

φMOFF​(P)≥φu>γ​age⁡(u,t),φMOFF​(P)≥φv>γ​age⁡(v,t).\varphi_{M^{\mathrm{OFF}}}(P)\geq\varphi_{u}>\gamma\operatorname{age}(u,t),\qquad\varphi_{M^{\mathrm{OFF}}}(P)\geq\varphi_{v}>\gamma\operatorname{age}(v,t). (5.2)

5.2 Computing Minimum Augmenting Paths

The graph HH of Section 3.1 relies on a fixed bipartition. We instead obtain the minimum augmenting paths from minimum-weight perfect matchings in general graphs. Consider a state with offline matching MM, and let UU be the set of requests saturated by MM. For two distinct free requests uu and vv, let Gu​vG_{uv} be the complete graph on U∪{u,v}U\cup\{u,v\} with edge weights

wM​(e)={D⁡(e),e∈M,γ​D​(e),e∉M.w_{M}(e)=\begin{cases}D(e),&e\in M,\\ \gamma D(e),&e\notin M.\end{cases}

For every perfect matching NN in Gu​vG_{uv}, the edge set N△MN\mathbin{\triangle}M consists of one MM-augmenting path from uu to vv and vertex-disjoint simple MM-alternating even cycles.

To update the minimum augmenting paths and the minimum γ\gamma-net-costs in Events RA and AU, the algorithm performs the following two steps.

  1. 1.

    For every pair of distinct free requests uu and vv, compute a minimum-weight perfect matching Nu​vN_{uv} in Gu​vG_{uv}, and let Qu​vQ_{uv} be the MM-augmenting path from uu to vv in Nu​v△MN_{uv}\mathbin{\triangle}M.

  2. 2.

    For every free request uu, choose a free request v≠uv\neq u that minimizes φM​(Qu​v)\varphi_{M}(Q_{uv}), and set Pu=Qu​vP_{u}=Q_{uv} and φu=φM​(Qu​v)\varphi_{u}=\varphi_{M}(Q_{uv}). If uu is the only free request, set φu=+∞\varphi_{u}=+\infty.

We now show that the two steps compute the minimum augmenting path PuP_{u} and the minimum γ\gamma-net-cost φu\varphi_{u} of every free request uu. Because Step 2 minimizes φM​(Qu​v)\varphi_{M}(Q_{uv}) over vv, it suffices to show that Qu​vQ_{uv} minimizes the γ\gamma-net-cost among all MM-augmenting paths from uu to vv. We first relate the weights in Gu​vG_{uv} to γ\gamma-net-costs.

Lemma 5.2.

Let MM be the offline matching at some state, and let uu and vv be distinct free requests. Every perfect matching NN in Gu​vG_{uv} satisfies wM​(N)−wM​(M)=φM​(N△M)w_{M}(N)-w_{M}(M)=\varphi_{M}(N\mathbin{\triangle}M).

Proof.

We have

wM​(N)−wM​(M)=γ​D​(N∖M)+D⁡(N∩M)−D⁡(M)=γ​D​(N∖M)−D⁡(M∖N)=φM​(N△M).w_{M}(N)-w_{M}(M)=\gamma D(N\setminus M)+D(N\cap M)-D(M)=\gamma D(N\setminus M)-D(M\setminus N)=\varphi_{M}(N\mathbin{\triangle}M).

∎

For every MM-augmenting path PP from uu to vv, the matching M△PM\mathbin{\triangle}P is a perfect matching in Gu​vG_{uv}, and Lemma 5.2 gives wM​(M△P)=wM​(M)+φM​(P)w_{M}(M\mathbin{\triangle}P)=w_{M}(M)+\varphi_{M}(P). Thus, to show that Qu​vQ_{uv} minimizes the γ\gamma-net-cost among all MM-augmenting paths from uu to vv, it suffices to show that M△Qu​vM\mathbin{\triangle}Q_{uv} is a minimum-weight perfect matching in Gu​vG_{uv}.

The matching Nu​vN_{uv} is a minimum-weight perfect matching in Gu​vG_{uv}. It differs from M△Qu​vM\mathbin{\triangle}Q_{uv} only on the alternating cycles of Nu​v△MN_{uv}\mathbin{\triangle}M. Lemma 5.3 shows that if no simple MM-alternating even cycle has negative γ\gamma-net-cost, these cycles cannot make Nu​vN_{uv} lighter than M△Qu​vM\mathbin{\triangle}Q_{uv}, so M△Qu​vM\mathbin{\triangle}Q_{uv} is also a minimum-weight perfect matching. Lemma 5.5 shows by induction on the events that the offline matching satisfies this condition at every state.

Lemma 5.3.

Let MM be the offline matching at some state, and suppose that every simple MM-alternating even cycle has nonnegative γ\gamma-net-cost. Then for every pair of distinct free requests uu and vv, the matching M△Qu​vM\mathbin{\triangle}Q_{uv} is a minimum-weight perfect matching in Gu​vG_{uv}.

Proof.

The edge set Nu​v△MN_{uv}\mathbin{\triangle}M consists of Qu​vQ_{uv} and simple MM-alternating even cycles, and each of these cycles has nonnegative γ\gamma-net-cost by assumption. Because φM\varphi_{M} is additive over disjoint edge sets, Lemma 5.2 gives

wM​(M△Qu​v)−wM​(M)=φM​(Qu​v)≤φM​(Nu​v△M)=wM​(Nu​v)−wM​(M).w_{M}(M\mathbin{\triangle}Q_{uv})-w_{M}(M)=\varphi_{M}(Q_{uv})\leq\varphi_{M}(N_{uv}\mathbin{\triangle}M)=w_{M}(N_{uv})-w_{M}(M).

Because M△Qu​vM\mathbin{\triangle}Q_{uv} is a perfect matching in Gu​vG_{uv}, it is a minimum-weight perfect matching in Gu​vG_{uv}. ∎

The induction step of Lemma 5.5 compares γ\gamma-net-costs with respect to the offline matchings before and after an augmentation, and we make this comparison edge by edge. For a matching LL and an edge ee, let cL​(e)=−D​(e)c_{L}(e)=-D(e) if e∈Le\in L and cL​(e)=γ​D​(e)c_{L}(e)=\gamma D(e) otherwise. Then cL​(e)c_{L}(e) is the γ\gamma-net-cost of switching ee with respect to LL, and φL​(F)\varphi_{L}(F) is the sum of cL​(e)c_{L}(e) over e∈Fe\in F.

Lemma 5.4.

Let MM and M′M^{\prime} be matchings, and let Q=M△M′Q=M\mathbin{\triangle}M^{\prime}.

  1. (a)

    Every edge e∉Qe\notin Q satisfies cM′​(e)=cM​(e)c_{M^{\prime}}(e)=c_{M}(e).

  2. (b)

    Every edge e∈Qe\in Q satisfies cM​(e)+cM′​(e)=(γ−1)​D​(e)c_{M}(e)+c_{M^{\prime}}(e)=(\gamma-1)D(e).

Proof.

(a) Because Q=M△M′Q=M\mathbin{\triangle}M^{\prime}, an edge outside QQ belongs to MM if and only if it belongs to M′M^{\prime}.

(b) An edge e∈Qe\in Q belongs to exactly one of MM and M′M^{\prime}. Thus, one of cM​(e)c_{M}(e) and cM′​(e)c_{M^{\prime}}(e) is −D⁡(e)-D(e), and the other is γ​D​(e)\gamma D(e). ∎

Lemma 5.5.

At every state of non-bipartite VRM, every simple MOFFM^{\mathrm{OFF}}-alternating even cycle CC satisfies φMOFF​(C)≥0\varphi_{M^{\mathrm{OFF}}}(C)\geq 0.

Proof.

We use induction on the events. Initially, MOFFM^{\mathrm{OFF}} is empty, so there is no alternating cycle. Every vertex of an alternating cycle is saturated, and a newly arriving request is free. Thus, an arrival preserves the statement.

Consider an augmentation for a free request uu, and let vv be the free request chosen for uu in Step 2, so that the augmentation is along Qu​vQ_{uv}. Let MM be the offline matching before the augmentation, and let M′=M△Qu​vM^{\prime}=M\mathbin{\triangle}Q_{uv}. By the induction hypothesis and Lemma 5.3, M′M^{\prime} is a minimum-weight perfect matching in Gu​vG_{uv}.

Suppose, for contradiction, that some simple M′M^{\prime}-alternating even cycle CC satisfies φM′​(C)<0\varphi_{M^{\prime}}(C)<0. Because CC is M′M^{\prime}-alternating, N=M′△CN=M^{\prime}\mathbin{\triangle}C is a matching that saturates the same requests as M′M^{\prime}, so NN is also a perfect matching in Gu​vG_{uv}. Because M′M^{\prime} is a minimum-weight perfect matching in Gu​vG_{uv}, it suffices to show that wM​(N)<wM​(M′)w_{M}(N)<w_{M}(M^{\prime}) to reach a contradiction.

We have N△M=M′△C△M=M△Qu​v△C△M=Qu​v△CN\mathbin{\triangle}M=M^{\prime}\mathbin{\triangle}C\mathbin{\triangle}M=M\mathbin{\triangle}Q_{uv}\mathbin{\triangle}C\mathbin{\triangle}M=Q_{uv}\mathbin{\triangle}C and M′△M=Qu​vM^{\prime}\mathbin{\triangle}M=Q_{uv}. Applying Lemma 5.2 to NN and to M′M^{\prime}, we obtain

wM​(N)−wM​(M′)\displaystyle w_{M}(N)-w_{M}(M^{\prime}) =(wM​(N)−wM​(M))−(wM​(M′)−wM​(M))\displaystyle=\bigl(w_{M}(N)-w_{M}(M)\bigr)-\bigl(w_{M}(M^{\prime})-w_{M}(M)\bigr)
=φM​(Qu​v△C)−φM​(Qu​v)\displaystyle=\varphi_{M}(Q_{uv}\mathbin{\triangle}C)-\varphi_{M}(Q_{uv})
=∑e∈C∖Qu​vcM​(e)−∑e∈Qu​v∩CcM​(e).\displaystyle=\sum_{e\in C\setminus Q_{uv}}c_{M}(e)-\sum_{e\in Q_{uv}\cap C}c_{M}(e).

Because Qu​v=M△M′Q_{uv}=M\mathbin{\triangle}M^{\prime}, Lemma 5.4(a) gives cM​(e)=cM′​(e)c_{M}(e)=c_{M^{\prime}}(e) for every e∈C∖Qu​ve\in C\setminus Q_{uv}, and Lemma 5.4(b) gives −cM​(e)=cM′​(e)−(γ−1)​D​(e)-c_{M}(e)=c_{M^{\prime}}(e)-(\gamma-1)D(e) for every e∈Qu​v∩Ce\in Q_{uv}\cap C. Therefore,

wM​(N)−wM​(M′)\displaystyle w_{M}(N)-w_{M}(M^{\prime}) =∑e∈C∖Qu​vcM′​(e)+∑e∈Qu​v∩C(cM′​(e)−(γ−1)​D​(e))\displaystyle=\sum_{e\in C\setminus Q_{uv}}c_{M^{\prime}}(e)+\sum_{e\in Q_{uv}\cap C}\bigl(c_{M^{\prime}}(e)-(\gamma-1)D(e)\bigr)
=φM′​(C)−(γ−1)​D​(Qu​v∩C)<0,\displaystyle=\varphi_{M^{\prime}}(C)-(\gamma-1)D(Q_{uv}\cap C)<0,

where the inequality uses φM′​(C)<0\varphi_{M^{\prime}}(C)<0 and γ>1\gamma>1. ∎

5.3 Bounding the Total Cost by the Total Waiting Time

Let trt_{r} be the time when request rr is matched, and let Rfree​(t)R_{\mathrm{free}}(t) be the set of free requests at time tt. The total waiting time of all requests is

WR=∑r∈R(tr−ar)=∫0∞|Rfree​(t)|​𝑑t,W_{R}=\sum_{r\in R}(t_{r}-a_{r})=\int_{0}^{\infty}|R_{\mathrm{free}}(t)|\,dt,

where the second equality holds because each free request incurs one unit of waiting cost per unit of time. The following lemma is the counterpart of Lemma 4.1. Its proof counts the waiting times of both endpoints of each output pair.

Lemma 5.6.

Non-bipartite VRM satisfies

ALG≤2​γγ−1​WR.\operatorname{ALG}\leq\frac{2\gamma}{\gamma-1}W_{R}.
Proof.

As in the proof of Lemma 4.1, let PiP_{i} be the path used in the iith augmentation, let MiM_{i} be the offline matching right before it, and write Di+=D⁡(Pi∖Mi)D_{i}^{+}=D(P_{i}\setminus M_{i}), Di−=D⁡(Pi∩Mi)D_{i}^{-}=D(P_{i}\cap M_{i}), and φi=γ​Di+−Di−\varphi_{i}=\gamma D_{i}^{+}-D_{i}^{-}. Let uiu_{i} be the request that initiates this augmentation, let viv_{i} be the other endpoint of PiP_{i}, and let tit_{i} be the time of this augmentation. Define

S=∑i=1m(ti−aui),T=∑i=1m(ti−avi).S=\sum_{i=1}^{m}(t_{i}-a_{u_{i}}),\qquad T=\sum_{i=1}^{m}(t_{i}-a_{v_{i}}).

By Eq. (5.1), φi≤γ⁡(ti−aui)\varphi_{i}\leq\gamma(t_{i}-a_{u_{i}}) for every ii, so ∑iφi≤γ​S\sum_{i}\varphi_{i}\leq\gamma S. Because the iith augmentation changes the total TA distance of MOFFM^{\mathrm{OFF}} by Di+−Di−D_{i}^{+}-D_{i}^{-}, the sum ∑i(Di+−Di−)\sum_{i}(D_{i}^{+}-D_{i}^{-}) is the total TA distance of the final offline matching, so it is nonnegative. Because (γ−1)​(Di++Di−)+(γ+1)​(Di+−Di−)=2​φi(\gamma-1)(D_{i}^{+}+D_{i}^{-})+(\gamma+1)(D_{i}^{+}-D_{i}^{-})=2\varphi_{i} for every ii, we have

∑i=1m(Di++Di−)=2γ−1​∑i=1mφi−γ+1γ−1​∑i=1m(Di+−Di−)≤2​γγ−1​S.\sum_{i=1}^{m}(D_{i}^{+}+D_{i}^{-})=\frac{2}{\gamma-1}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\varphi_{i}-\frac{\gamma+1}{\gamma-1}\sum_{i=1}^{m}(D_{i}^{+}-D_{i}^{-})\leq\frac{2\gamma}{\gamma-1}S.

By the triangle inequality and ti≥max⁡{aui,avi}t_{i}\geq\max\{a_{u_{i}},a_{v_{i}}\}, the cost of output pair ui​viu_{i}v_{i} is

d⁡(xui,xvi)+(ti−aui)+(ti−avi)\displaystyle d(x_{u_{i}},x_{v_{i}})+(t_{i}-a_{u_{i}})+(t_{i}-a_{v_{i}}) =D⁡(ui,vi)+2​(ti−max⁡{aui,avi})\displaystyle=D(u_{i},v_{i})+2\bigl(t_{i}-\max\{a_{u_{i}},a_{v_{i}}\}\bigr)
≤Di++Di−+2​(ti−avi).\displaystyle\leq D_{i}^{+}+D_{i}^{-}+2(t_{i}-a_{v_{i}}).

Summing over the pairs gives

ALG≤2​γγ−1​S+2​T≤2​γγ−1​(S+T)=2​γγ−1​WR,\operatorname{ALG}\leq\frac{2\gamma}{\gamma-1}S+2T\leq\frac{2\gamma}{\gamma-1}(S+T)=\frac{2\gamma}{\gamma-1}W_{R},

where the second inequality uses γ>1\gamma>1 and the equality uses S+T=WRS+T=W_{R}. ∎

5.4 Charging the Waiting Time to the Optimal Matching

We now bound WRW_{R} by adapting the charging scheme in Sections 4.2–4.4. Fix a minimum-cost perfect matching M∗M^{*} on RR under DD, so that D⁡(M∗)=OPTD(M^{*})=\operatorname{OPT}, and write MtM_{t} for the offline matching at time tt. Consider a free request uu at time tt. Because uu is not saturated by MtM_{t} and M∗M^{*} is perfect, the component of Mt△M∗M_{t}\mathbin{\triangle}M^{*} containing uu is an MtM_{t}-augmenting path from uu to another request. We call this path the optimal path of uu at time tt, denote it by Pu∗​(t)P^{*}_{u}(t), and call its last vertex the terminal request. The terminal request is not saturated by MtM_{t}, so it is either free or not yet arrived.

Lemma 5.7.

Let uu and ww be distinct free requests at time tt. If ww is the terminal request of Pu∗​(t)P^{*}_{u}(t), then Pu∗​(t)P^{*}_{u}(t) and Pw∗​(t)P^{*}_{w}(t) have the same edges. Otherwise, Pu∗​(t)P^{*}_{u}(t) and Pw∗​(t)P^{*}_{w}(t) share no edge. Moreover, every interior vertex of an optimal path has arrived.

Proof.

The paths Pu∗​(t)P^{*}_{u}(t) and Pw∗​(t)P^{*}_{w}(t) are the components of Mt△M∗M_{t}\mathbin{\triangle}M^{*} containing uu and ww, respectively. If ww is the terminal request of Pu∗​(t)P^{*}_{u}(t), the two components coincide, so the two paths have the same edges. Otherwise, ww is neither uu nor the terminal request of Pu∗​(t)P^{*}_{u}(t). Because ww is not saturated by MtM_{t}, it is not an interior vertex of Pu∗​(t)P^{*}_{u}(t) either. Hence ww is not on Pu∗​(t)P^{*}_{u}(t), and the two components are different and share no edge. Next, an optimal path alternates between edges of M∗M^{*} and edges of MtM_{t}, so each of its interior vertices is incident to an edge of MtM_{t}. Because MtM_{t} is a matching on the requests that have arrived, every interior vertex has arrived. ∎

The following lemma is the counterpart of Lemma 4.4.

Lemma 5.8.

Fix a stable time tt and a free request uu such that the terminal request of P∗=Pu∗​(t)P^{*}=P^{*}_{u}(t) has arrived, and let D∗=D⁡(P∗∩M∗)D^{*}=D(P^{*}\cap M^{*}). Then

D∗≥age⁡(u,t)andD∗≥age⁡(z,t)γ+1​ for every vertex z of P∗.D^{*}\geq\operatorname{age}(u,t)\qquad\text{and}\qquad D^{*}\geq\frac{\operatorname{age}(z,t)}{\gamma+1}\ \text{ for every vertex $z$ of $P^{*}$.}
Proof.

Let D−=D⁡(P∗∩Mt)D^{-}=D(P^{*}\cap M_{t}), so that D⁡(P∗)=D∗+D−D(P^{*})=D^{*}+D^{-}. By Lemma 5.7 and the assumption, all vertices of P∗P^{*} have arrived. The terminal request of P∗P^{*} is not saturated by MtM_{t}, so it is free. Thus, P∗P^{*} is an MtM_{t}-augmenting path between two free requests, and Eq. (5.2) gives γ​D∗−D−=φMt​(P∗)>γ​age⁡(u,t)\gamma D^{*}-D^{-}=\varphi_{M_{t}}(P^{*})>\gamma\operatorname{age}(u,t). This is the inequality that the proof of Lemma 4.4 obtains from Lemma 3.3. The rest of that proof then applies verbatim, with uu and zz in place of rr and vv. ∎

Because there are only finitely many event times, the waiting cost incurred at them is zero. Thus, it suffices to charge the waiting cost at stable times. We consider a stable time tt and a free request uu, and we charge the waiting cost of uu as follows.

Case 1: the terminal request of Pu∗​(t)P^{*}_{u}(t) has not arrived.

We charge the waiting cost of uu to the last edge e=p​ve=pv of Pu∗​(t)P^{*}_{u}(t), where vv is the terminal request. This edge belongs to M∗M^{*}. By Lemma 5.7, pp has arrived, since it is uu or an interior vertex of Pu∗​(t)P^{*}_{u}(t). Because vv has not arrived, it is not free. Thus, by Lemma 5.7, no other free request has an optimal path containing ee, and ee is charged at rate at most one. Let W1W_{1} be the total waiting cost charged in this case over all requests and over time.

Fix an edge e=p​v∈M∗e=pv\in M^{*}, where ap≤ava_{p}\leq a_{v}. Whenever ee is charged in this case at time tt, we have ap≤t<ava_{p}\leq t<a_{v}. Because the charge rate is at most one, the total charge to ee in this case is at most av−ap≤D⁡(p,v)a_{v}-a_{p}\leq D(p,v). Summing over all edges of M∗M^{*} gives W1≤∑p​v∈M∗D⁡(p,v)=OPTW_{1}\leq\sum_{pv\in M^{*}}D(p,v)=\operatorname{OPT}.

Case 2: the terminal request of Pu∗​(t)P^{*}_{u}(t) has arrived.

Let D∗=D⁡(Pu∗​(t)∩M∗)D^{*}=D(P^{*}_{u}(t)\cap M^{*}) be the total TA distance of the edges of M∗M^{*} on Pu∗​(t)P^{*}_{u}(t). For each edge e∈Pu∗​(t)∩M∗e\in P^{*}_{u}(t)\cap M^{*}, we charge the waiting cost of uu to ee at rate D⁡(e)/D∗D(e)/D^{*}. Lemma 5.8 gives D∗≥age⁡(u,t)D^{*}\geq\operatorname{age}(u,t), and age⁡(u,t)>0\operatorname{age}(u,t)>0 because no request arrives at the stable time tt. Thus, the rate is well defined. For each edge e∈M∗e\in M^{*}, let qe​(t)q_{e}(t) be the sum of the charge rates assigned to ee in this case by all free requests at a stable time tt, with qe​(t)=0q_{e}(t)=0 at event times.

Fix an edge e∈M∗e\in M^{*}. Choose one endpoint zz of ee, and let be=azb_{e}=a_{z}. Consider a stable time tt with qe​(t)>0q_{e}(t)>0. Let ue​(t)u_{e}(t) be a request charging ee at time tt, let Pe∗​(t)=Pue​(t)∗​(t)P^{*}_{e}(t)=P^{*}_{u_{e}(t)}(t) be its optimal path, and let De∗​(t)=D⁡(Pe∗​(t)∩M∗)D^{*}_{e}(t)=D(P^{*}_{e}(t)\cap M^{*}). By Lemma 5.7, the terminal request of Pe∗​(t)P^{*}_{e}(t) is the only other request that can charge ee at time tt, and its optimal path has the same edges as Pe∗​(t)P^{*}_{e}(t). Thus, at most two requests charge ee, and each of them charges ee at rate D⁡(e)/De∗​(t)D(e)/D^{*}_{e}(t). Hence qe​(t)≤2​D​(e)/De∗​(t)q_{e}(t)\leq 2D(e)/D^{*}_{e}(t).

The second bound of Lemma 5.8, applied to ue​(t)u_{e}(t), gives De∗​(t)≥(t−be)/(γ+1)D^{*}_{e}(t)\geq(t-b_{e})/(\gamma+1). Because De∗​(t)≤D⁡(M∗)=OPTD^{*}_{e}(t)\leq D(M^{*})=\operatorname{OPT}, this bound gives t≤be+(γ+1)​OPTt\leq b_{e}+(\gamma+1)\operatorname{OPT}. As in the proof of Lemma 4.5, we have

qe​(t)\displaystyle q_{e}(t) ≤min⁡{2,2​(γ+1)​D​(e)t−be}\displaystyle\leq\min\Bigl\{2,\,\frac{2(\gamma+1)D(e)}{t-b_{e}}\Bigr\} if t∈(be,be+(γ+1)OPT],\displaystyle\text{if }t\in(b_{e},\,b_{e}+(\gamma+1)\operatorname{OPT}], (5.3)
qe​(t)\displaystyle q_{e}(t) =0\displaystyle=0 otherwise.\displaystyle\text{otherwise}.

Integrating as in Eq. (4.7), we have

∫0∞qe​(t)​𝑑t≤2​(γ+1)​(OPTm+D⁡(e)​ln⁡m).\int_{0}^{\infty}q_{e}(t)\,dt\leq 2(\gamma+1)\Bigl(\frac{\operatorname{OPT}}{m}+D(e)\ln m\Bigr).

5.5 Proof of Theorem 5.1

Adding the charge W1W_{1} in Case 1 and the charge to all edges in Case 2, we obtain

WR\displaystyle W_{R} =W1+∑e∈M∗∫0∞qe​(t)​𝑑t\displaystyle=W_{1}+\sum_{e\in M^{*}}\int_{0}^{\infty}q_{e}(t)\,dt
≤OPT+∑e∈M∗2​(γ+1)​(OPTm+D⁡(e)​ln⁡m)\displaystyle\leq\operatorname{OPT}+\sum_{e\in M^{*}}2(\gamma+1)\Bigl(\frac{\operatorname{OPT}}{m}+D(e)\ln m\Bigr)
=[1+2​(γ+1)​(1+ln⁡m)]​OPT.\displaystyle=\bigl[1+2(\gamma+1)(1+\ln m)\bigr]\operatorname{OPT}.

The last equality holds because M∗M^{*} has mm edges and ∑e∈M∗D⁡(e)=OPT\sum_{e\in M^{*}}D(e)=\operatorname{OPT}. Combining this bound with Lemma 5.6 gives

ALG≤2​γγ−1​[1+2​(γ+1)​(1+ln⁡m)]​OPT.\operatorname{ALG}\leq\frac{2\gamma}{\gamma-1}\bigl[1+2(\gamma+1)(1+\ln m)\bigr]\operatorname{OPT}.

For γ=2\gamma=2, the coefficient is 4​[1+6​(1+ln⁡m)]=28+24​ln⁡m4[1+6(1+\ln m)]=28+24\ln m. Finally, the algorithm does not need to know the metric space or mm in advance, since mm, M∗M^{*}, and OPT\operatorname{OPT} are used only in the analysis.

6 Concluding Remarks

Several ingredients of the analysis are shared with previous analyses of RM and VRM. The bound on the total length of the augmenting paths in Lemma 4.1 is from [42, 34], and the optimal-path construction in Section 4.2 and the path-length comparison in the proof of Lemma 4.4 are from [40, 34]. The distinguishing feature of our analysis is that it charges waiting time over time rather than net-cost per augmentation. In particular, it does not use the geometric decomposition of the metric space that underlies the analyses in [40, 34], and it does not use the monotonicity of the minimum net-cost under augmentations [34, Lemma 4.2].

Without delays, no deterministic algorithm is polylogarithmic-competitive in high dimensions. In dd-dimensional Euclidean space, every deterministic algorithm for the MBPM problem has competitive ratio Ω⁡(m1−1/d)\Omega(m^{1-1/d}) [43, 40]. In contrast, VRM, which is built on RM, is O⁡(log⁡m)O(\log m)-competitive for the MBPMD problem in any metric space. From this perspective, allowing delays makes matching easier for deterministic algorithms, although the two problems are not directly comparable.

AI Usage and Methodology

Background.

After our earlier paper on VRM [34], we did not expect VRM to be polylogarithmic-competitive, because RM, on which it is based, is not polylogarithmic-competitive in high dimensions (see Section 6). We therefore did not plan to analyze VRM further. The deterministic O⁡(log5⁡m)O(\log^{5}m)-competitive algorithm of Dufay and Wattenhofer for the MPMD problem [21] motivated us to revisit the MBPMD problem. In October 2025, we tried to design a new algorithm for the MBPMD problem with GPT-5 (OpenAI) and substantial human input, but these attempts failed.

How the result was found.

In September 2026, we first gave Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic) a single prompt that included our paper on VRM [34]. In this prompt, we asked the model to read that paper and then to consider the same problem, the MBPMD problem on the line, and either to design a deterministic polylogarithmic-competitive online algorithm or to give a lower bound showing that no such algorithm exists. This attempt failed. We then gave the same prompt to GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI) in the same working directory, which still contained the notes and code of that attempt. We expected that, if the model succeeded, it would design a new algorithm.

What GPT-6 Astra contributed.

Instead, GPT-6 Astra proved that VRM is O⁡(log⁡m)O(\log m)-competitive in any metric space, although the problem was posed on the line. There was almost no human input. We repeatedly asked the model to continue until the proof was complete. The core of its proof is the charging argument now in Sections 4.2–4.4. In a separate session, we asked the same model to extend the result to the MPMD problem, again with almost no human input. The extension in Section 5 comes from that session.

We found afterwards that GPT-6 Astra’s notes cite the notes of the Claude Fable 5.1 attempt and that its scripts reuse the code of that attempt. Claude Fable 5.1’s notes already distinguished the two cases of Section 4.2. They contained a charging scheme for Case 1 but none that bounded the waiting cost in Case 2.

Verification and presentation.

We verified the proofs found by GPT-6 Astra by rewriting them with Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), which also helped us simplify and present the results and edit the text. Claude Fable 5.1 also checked an early version of Section 5 and revised its notation. We checked every step of the rewritten proofs ourselves. This paper presents the rewritten proofs, which include one slight improvement. The next paragraph describes it.

We first explained to Claude Opus 5.5 our own interpretation of the original proof for the MBPMD problem found by GPT-6 Astra and then discussed how one might arrive at this proof. After this discussion, Claude Opus 5.5 noticed that, in the proof of Lemma 4.5, the charge rate qe​(t)q_{e}(t) can also be bounded by 11 (see Eq. (4.6)). This observation simplifies both original proofs found by GPT-6 Astra and improves the resulting competitive ratios.

While rewriting the proofs, we found another improvement, which this paper does not use. Using MV servers and [34, Lemma 4.1], we can show that Case 1 is not needed. For γ=2\gamma=2, this improves the ratio in Theorem 1.1 from 24+18​ln⁡m24+18\ln m to 18+18​ln⁡m18+18\ln m. We later discovered that the original proof found by GPT-6 Astra already contains this argument.

However, because the proof with Case 1 does not use MV servers, it is simpler. Moreover, Section 5 adapts it to the MPMD problem, whereas the other improvement relies on [34, Lemma 4.1], which does not extend to the MPMD problem. For these reasons, we present the proof with Case 1.

Appendix A Validity of the Algorithm

In this appendix, we prove Lemma 3.1. The proof is similar to the corresponding proofs for RM [42] and VRM [34]. In particular, it uses the relaxed dual feasibility and matched-edge tightness conditions of [42] and [34, Section 3.2.1, Invariants (I1) and (I4)].

Proof of Lemma 3.1.

We prove by induction that HH has no negative cycle. Initially, HH has no cycle. When a request arrives, it is free and has no incoming edge. Similarly, a newly arrived server has no outgoing edge. Thus, newly arrived vertices cannot create a directed cycle.

Next, consider an augmentation and assume that there is no negative cycle before the augmentation. We first work with the state right before the augmentation. Let TT be the nonempty set of free servers. Every request has a directed edge to a server in TT, and every matched server has a directed edge to the request matched to it. Thus, every arrived vertex is in TT or has a directed path to TT. For each arrived vertex vv, let ℓ⁡(v)\ell(v) be its shortest distance to TT in HH. Because there is no negative cycle, this distance is finite and is attained by a simple path. Also, ℓ⁡(s)=0\ell(s)=0 for every s∈Ts\in T.

To show that the augmentation does not create a negative cycle, we assign a real-valued variable to each arrived vertex as follows:

zr=ℓ⁡(r)(r∈R),zs=−ℓ⁡(s)(s∈S).z_{r}=\ell(r)\quad(r\in R),\qquad z_{s}=-\ell(s)\quad(s\in S).

Thus, zr+zs=ℓ⁡(r)−ℓ⁡(s)z_{r}+z_{s}=\ell(r)-\ell(s) for every edge r​srs at this state.

For any unmatched edge r​srs, the shortest-distance inequality gives

zr+zs≤γ​D​(r,s).z_{r}+z_{s}\leq\gamma D(r,s). (A.1)

For any matched edge r​srs, the only outgoing edge of ss is the directed edge from ss to rr, so ℓ⁡(s)=−D⁡(r,s)+ℓ⁡(r)\ell(s)=-D(r,s)+\ell(r). Thus,

zr+zs=D⁡(r,s)≤γ​D​(r,s).z_{r}+z_{s}=D(r,s)\leq\gamma D(r,s). (A.2)

Hence, Eq. (A.1) holds for every edge.

Let PP be the minimum augmenting path used in the augmentation. Because PP is a shortest path from its first vertex to TT in HH, every directed edge of PP from uu to vv satisfies ℓ⁡(u)=w+ℓ⁡(v)\ell(u)=w+\ell(v), where ww is the weight of this edge in HH. A forward edge r​srs of PP is directed from rr to ss and has weight γ​D​(r,s)\gamma D(r,s). Thus, it satisfies zr+zs=ℓ⁡(r)−ℓ⁡(s)=γ​D​(r,s)z_{r}+z_{s}=\ell(r)-\ell(s)=\gamma D(r,s). These forward edges are exactly the edges that become matched in this augmentation.

After the augmentation, each request rr on PP is matched by the forward edge r​srs of PP that leaves rr. We decrease zrz_{r} by (γ−1)​D​(r,s)(\gamma-1)D(r,s), and all other variables remain unchanged. Because only request variables decrease, Eq. (A.1) continues to hold for every edge. Each newly matched edge r​srs had zr+zs=γ​D​(r,s)z_{r}+z_{s}=\gamma D(r,s) before this update, so it now has zr+zs=γ​D​(r,s)−(γ−1)​D​(r,s)=D⁡(r,s)z_{r}+z_{s}=\gamma D(r,s)-(\gamma-1)D(r,s)=D(r,s), and Eq. (A.2) holds for it. For an old matched edge that remains in the matching, neither endpoint is on PP, so Eq. (A.2) also continues to hold.

Consider any cycle CC in HH after the augmentation, and let C+C^{+} and C−C^{-} be the sets of unmatched and matched edges of CC, respectively. The weight of CC is γ​D​(C+)−D⁡(C−)\gamma D(C^{+})-D(C^{-}). By Eq. (A.1) for the edges in C+C^{+} and Eq. (A.2) for the edges in C−C^{-}, we have

γ​D​(C+)−D⁡(C−)≥∑r​s∈C+(zr+zs)−∑r​s∈C−(zr+zs)=0.\gamma D(C^{+})-D(C^{-})\geq\sum_{rs\in C^{+}}(z_{r}+z_{s})-\sum_{rs\in C^{-}}(z_{r}+z_{s})=0.

The last equality holds because unmatched and matched edges alternate along CC, so every vertex of CC is incident to exactly one edge in C+C^{+} and exactly one edge in C−C^{-}. Thus, CC has nonnegative weight, which completes the induction. ∎
